name: Powdery mildew
scientificName: Golovinomyces ambrosiae / Podosphaera macularis complex on Cannabis sativa
summary: Cannabis powdery mildew is a disease class marked by superficial whitish mycelium and conidia that expand across living foliage and sometimes petioles, stems, bracts, or flowers. The phenotype can strongly support a powdery-mildew triage label, but a photograph cannot distinguish Golovinomyces ambrosiae from Podosphaera macularis, exclude co-infection, or prove that white material is fungal.
affectedParts: upper leaf surface and colony margin
lower leaf surface paired to the same marked leaf
immature first true leaves on susceptible plants
mature fan leaves across canopy positions
adjacent symptom-negative tissue used for serial comparison
indicators: Small irregular whitish colonies sit superficially on living Cannabis tissue and show a powdery, diffuse, or felt-like texture rather than only internal loss of green color.
Paired views of a marked leaf show whether colonies occur on the upper surface, lower surface, or both; a single overexposed surface is insufficient.
At an active colony edge, magnification resolves branching superficial hyphae, upright conidiophores, or conidia rather than crystalline residue, droplets, trichome heads, or silk threads.
Serial fixed-area images show colonies enlarging, merging, or appearing on additional leaves instead of remaining fixed to a one-time spray or abrasion pattern.
Coverage can progress from a few restricted colonies to broad white surface growth across leaves and then petioles or stems under sustained disease pressure.
Severe adult-plant disease can extend onto sugar leaves, flower bracts, or buds; dense surface growth must still be separated from normal glandular trichomes and internal flower molds.
Affected leaves can later yellow, become necrotic, or defoliate, but those secondary changes support powdery mildew only when linked to an active superficial colony.
Susceptible tissue can be affected from immature first true leaves through flowering, so canopy position and leaf age must be recorded rather than inferred from a nutrient-mobility rule.
exclusions: Foliar spray, sulfur, bicarbonate, mineral, or hard-water residue follows droplets or application geometry, can occur on pots or other nonliving surfaces, and lacks branching hyphae, conidiophores, and an advancing colony margin.
Normal glandular trichomes are repeated plant structures with stalks and heads anchored to flower or sugar-leaf tissue rather than an irregular spreading mycelial mat.
Spider-mite silk resolves as threads or sheets associated with mites, round eggs, cast skins, and feeding stippling rather than fungal hyphae and conidia.
Botrytis or another internal flower mold produces advancing tan or brown tissue decay, internal breakdown, or gray-brown sporulation rather than only superficial white colonies on living tissue.
Downy mildew is associated with angular chlorotic-to-necrotic lesions and corresponding gray-to-purplish underside sporulation rather than a freely spreading superficial white colony.
Leaf bleaching, genetic sectoring, nutrient chlorosis, and camera overexposure remain within tissue and do not resolve into hyphae or conidia under magnification.
Pollen, dust, lint, perlite, and plant fibers transfer or collect without a plant-linked advancing colony and lack compatible fungal structures.

A one-frame white patch disappears under corrected exposure or white balance, or repeated marked-tissue imaging shows no organism structure or expansion; retain an artifact or unresolved-material label.

progression.description: A clean image is symptom-negative only; resistant genotypes can suppress visible colonization, and visually clean tissue is not a universal pathogen-negative control.
A few small superficial white colonies appear on one or more marked surfaces. In the PM2 study scale, grade 1 represented restricted, nonspreading colonies covering less than 25% of the leaf.
Serial views show colonies enlarging or merging. Study grades 2 and 3 represented 25–50% and 50–75% leaf-area coverage, but those percentages remain experiment-specific.
Study grade 4 represented 75–100% leaf coverage; petioles, stems, sugar leaves, bracts, or buds may also be colonized under severe adult-plant pressure.
Leaves may yellow, become necrotic, or defoliate, and flower quality can decline; these effects require the active colony to preserve the powdery-mildew label.

lookAlikes: Foliar spray, sulfur, bicarbonate, or oil residue
Dust, pollen, lint, perlite, or plant fibers
Botrytis gray mold or bud rot
Penicillium or other internal flower mold
White rust or another sporulating pathogen
Genetic variegation or stable chlorotic sectoring
Camera overexposure, glare, or white-balance artifact
confirmation: Do not confirm powdery mildew or assign a species from one photograph or video; cap visual-only confidence at 0.30 and capture whole-canopy distribution plus paired upper- and lower-surface macros from the same marked symptomatic and adjacent apparently clean leaves.

At the active colony edge, use magnification to document branching superficial hyphae, conidiophores, and conidia; include a scale and side-lit video or a focus stack that separates fungal growth from crystals, droplets, trichomes, and silk.
Record whether material transfers when touched, but do not use wipe behavior alone as confirmation because residue, dust, pollen, and fungal spores can all move.

Revisit fixed leaves and colony margins at recorded intervals; new colony area or additional infected organs supports active disease, while unchanged white material without fungal structures remains unresolved.

For disease-class ground truth, link fresh tissue from the photographed plant and organ to qualified diagnostic-laboratory microscopy plus a validated molecular assay; for species-level ground truth, use sequence or species-specific evidence that can detect G. ambrosiae, P. macularis, or co-infection.

Record cultivar or genotype, plant age, stage, organ, canopy position, production setting, first-observed date, repeated fixed-area coverage, temperature, humidity, airflow, nearby infected plants, and every recent foliar input.

Treat absent colonies as a symptom-negative observation, not proof of resistance or pathogen absence; controlled resistance claims require replicated inoculation, a defined isolate or population, and appropriate susceptible controls.
immediateActions: Separate or flag affected plants, minimize handling and airflow disturbances that can disperse conidia, and preserve a fresh diagnostic sample before removal.
Map affected plants and organs, capture pre-intervention colony coverage, and inspect nearby plants on both leaf surfaces and flower-adjacent tissue.
correctivePlan: Use only legal, crop-, site-, and growth-stage-appropriate disease management selected for the production system; follow the product label and local testing requirements.
Remove heavily affected material without dispersing spores where permitted, clean tools and contact surfaces, and track new colony development rather than persistent old discoloration.
Review humidity, air movement, canopy density, intake material, and cross-room movement as epidemiological context without treating any single environmental reading as diagnostic proof.
prevention: Inspect incoming plants and clones under magnification and maintain cultivar/source identity so repeated susceptibility can be recognized.
Scout fixed leaves and flower-adjacent tissues across canopy zones, recording new colony area over time and retaining source-group identity for image sequences.
warnings: The 2019 Kentucky DOI originally identified Golovinomyces spadiceus; later taxonomy generally includes that name within G. ambrosiae. Preserve the original title and do not silently rewrite historical species labels.
At least two powdery-mildew fungi, Golovinomyces ambrosiae and Podosphaera macularis, have been PCR-confirmed on hemp, so disease-class imagery is not species-level ground truth.
The PM2 0-to-4 leaf-coverage scale is a controlled resistance-study scale, not a universal field severity, yield-loss, or intervention threshold.

Cultivar, genotype, pathogen isolate, organ, plant stage, and inoculum pressure can change visible severity; adult plants in one study sometimes appeared more susceptible than their earlier clone assay.
The March 2026 handbook describes mostly diffuse Golovinomyces colonies and denser Podosphaera growth in its example images, but density, organ, or field context must not be used to assign species.

The 2026 genome assembly came from heavily infected leaves of one greenhouse cultivar and one G. ambrosiae collection; it strengthens taxonomy and molecular resources but does not define a universal visual phenotype or resistance guarantee.
The linked CC BY 4.0 susceptible-versus-resistant Figure 2 is a shared-experiment composite. It remains training-ineligible, and the resistant panel is not an independent universal negative sample.
The three Pacific Northwest photographs have no item-level reuse license; their metadata may guide human review, but the files are not stored, displayed, or admitted to training.
Do not consume visibly mold-contaminated material, and do not apply unapproved products to Cannabis or flowering tissue.

sources.title: First Report of Powdery Mildew Caused by Golovinomyces spadiceus on Industrial Hemp (Cannabis sativa) in Kentucky
supportedClaims: The Kentucky report identified a powdery mildew on industrial hemp as Golovinomyces spadiceus using fungal morphology and ITS plus 28S sequence evidence.
The historical G. spadiceus name in this report is now generally treated within the amended G. ambrosiae concept; the DOI must not be cited as though its original title named G. ambrosiae.

sources.title: Characterization of Powdery Mildew Fungi Affecting Hemp in the Pacific Northwest
supportedClaims: Surveys of 74 hemp fields in Oregon and Washington across three time points in 2021 and 2022 found powdery mildew later in the season in Oregon but not at the early survey point.
Diagnostic PCR detected both Golovinomyces ambrosiae and Podosphaera macularis on hemp, so a white powdery-mildew phenotype does not resolve the causal species.
Among assayed survey samples, G. ambrosiae was much more frequent than P. macularis, but the regional and seasonal sample does not establish a universal species prior for other production systems.

sources.title: Discovery and Genetic Mapping of PM1, a Powdery Mildew Resistance Gene in Cannabis sativa L.
supportedClaims: Patchy white mycelial colonies developed on Cannabis foliage and flowers and were associated with reduced vigor, but colony presence did not by itself identify every possible powdery-mildew species.

In two segregating Cannabis populations, susceptible plants developed white colonies on leaves and stems within 45 days of germination under continuous inoculum pressure, while PM1-bearing plants showed complete resistance to the tested Pacific Northwest G. ambrosiae isolate.

Plants were followed through flowering, and 55 clonal replicates were reinfected to validate scores; resistance or absence of visible colonies in this experiment is genotype- and isolate-specific rather than a universal negative control.

Figure 2 is a CC BY 4.0 susceptible-versus-resistant Cannabis comparison; its panels share experimental source context and must not be treated as independent training samples without source grouping and review.

sources.title: Mapping and Characterization of a Novel Powdery Mildew Resistance Locus (PM2) in Cannabis sativa L.
sources.organization: Frontiers in Plant Science (Seifi et al.)
supportedClaims: The study used a leaf-area severity scale of 0 for no symptoms, 1 for less than 25% coverage with few restricted nonspreading colonies, 2 for 25–50%, 3 for 50–75%, and 4 for 75–100% powdery-mildew coverage.

Under severe adult-plant disease pressure, susceptible genotypes could show colonization of flower sugar leaves, petioles, and stem tissue; adult susceptibility sometimes exceeded the earlier clone-assay result.

PM2 resistance strongly suppressed conidia generation and involved a localized microscopic hypersensitive response without macroscopic chlorotic spots, so symptom-negative or visually clean tissue is not proof that all pathogen interaction is absent.
The scale and response were generated in controlled inoculation and resistance-mapping experiments and are not universal field severity, yield-loss, or intervention thresholds.

sources.title: Field Guide to Hemp (Cannabis sativa) Diseases
sources.publisher: University of Florida Institute of Food and Agricultural Sciences Extension
supportedClaims: On hemp, powdery fungal mycelium and spores can appear as whitish spots or patches on both leaf surfaces and can spread across leaves, petioles, stems, flower bracts, and buds within about a week under favorable conditions.
Increasing severity can lead to leaf necrosis and defoliation, while high humidity favors infection even though free leaf wetness is not required.

The guide recommends diagnostic-center confirmation for hemp diseases; its powdery-mildew image is credited to Nicole Gauthier and does not carry an explicit reusable-media license on the page, so it is not copied or indexed as training media here.

sources.title: Hemp (Cannabis sativa)-Powdery Mildew
sources.organization: Pacific Northwest Plant Disease Management Handbook
sources.publisher: Oregon State University, Washington State University, and University of Idaho Extension
supportedClaims: The March 2026 handbook reports Golovinomyces ambrosiae on greenhouse and field hemp in Oregon and natural field infection by Podosphaera macularis, while emphasizing that both are powdery-mildew fungi of Cannabis.

Susceptible plants can develop disease from immature first true leaves onward; whitish powdery colonies can occupy upper leaf surfaces and expand across whole leaves, petioles, flower bracts, and buds.

The handbook describes Golovinomyces colonies as small and mostly diffuse and a photographed Podosphaera infection as denser in hyphal growth and sporulation, but appearance alone is insufficient for a species label.
The three Cannabis photographs are credited to C. M. Ocamb or Taylor A. Bates and have no item-level reuse or automated-training license; they remain hidden metadata references and are not copied.

sources.title: Hybrid genome assembly of the cannabis powdery mildew agent Golovinomyces ambrosiae uncovers important resources for deciphering virulence factors
supportedClaims: The study generated the first hybrid genome assembly for the Cannabis powdery-mildew pathogen Golovinomyces ambrosiae from heavily infected leaves of one susceptible greenhouse cultivar.

Its synthesis treats G. ambrosiae and Podosphaera macularis as the currently supported powdery-mildew species on Cannabis and notes documented co-infection, reinforcing disease-class rather than image-based species labels.
Multi-locus evidence supports G. spadiceus and G. ambrosiae as one taxon, while G. ambrosiae remains genetically distinct from the broad historical G. cichoracearum concept.

The pathogen genome contains numerous candidate effectors and substantial repeat content; resistance linked to a host locus or one isolate must not be generalized to every pathogen population or visually clean plant.
